title: Piman languages - Wikipedia
text: Piman (or Tepiman) refers to a group of languages within the Uto-Aztecan family that are spoken by ethnic groups (including the Pima) spanning from Arizona in the north to Durango, Mexico in the south.

title: Pima Bajo people - Wikipedia
text: The Pima Bajo (Lower Pima) people are an Indigenous people of Mexico who reside in a mountainous region along the line between the states of Chihuahua and Sonora in northern Mexico.

title: Pima Bajo language - Wikipedia
text: Pima Bajo (Mountain Pima, Lowland Pima, Nevome) is a Mexican indigenous language of the Piman branch of the Uto-Aztecan language family, spoken by around 1,000 speakers in northern Mexico.

title: Pima Bajo Language and the Nevome Indian Tribe (O'ob No'ok...)
text: Pima Bajo (O:b No'ok, Nevome). Pima Bajo is a Uto-Aztecan language of Mexico, spoken today by a few hundred indigenous people in the mountains between Sonora and Chihuahua. There are two dialects of Pima Bajo, a Sonoran dialect and a Chihuahuan one.

title: Pima Bajo - PDF Drive
text: Pima Bajo is a Uto-Aztecan language from the Tepiman branch spoken by no more than 500 persons. The Pima Bajo country is located in the Southeastern part of Sonora Mexico, and also in the Central Western part of Chihuahua in Mexico.

title: Tohono O'odham (Papago) and Akimel O'odham (Pima)
text: It has two dialects, Tohono O'odham (also known as Papago) and Akimel O'odham (also known as Pima). Speakers of one of these dialects can fairly easily understand each other, just as speakers of American and Australian English can.

title: Languages | Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community
text: Within the Salt River Pima-Maricopa Indian Community (SRPMIC), two Indigenous languages — O’odham Ñiokĭ (Pima) and Piipaash Chuukwer (Maricopa) — carry the voices of generations past and present.
